comparison: Perfect agreement on C55. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the cautious interpretation of the interaction finding, acknowledging the n=1 limitation and treating it as appropriately preliminary.

Perfect agreement on C110-C112. Both evaluations strongly affirm the study's significance and contributions to the field, with peer reviewers calling it 'a critical step' and OpenEval confirming accurate characterization of accomplishments.

Strong agreement on peak expression timing (C4, C32). Both evaluations support the ~60-day finding with OpenEval noting sigmoid curve fitting (BIC=61.1) and peer reviewers describing 'exceptional evidence' for this discovery.

Strong agreement on hM4Di stability (C5, C34, C56). Both evaluations affirm stable expression for up to 2 years for hM4Di, with OpenEval noting 16 injection sites across 11 monkeys and peer reviewers confirming 'up to 1.5 years' stability.

Strong agreement on hM3Dq variability (C36, C37, C56). Both evaluations accept the greater variability and decline pattern for hM3Dq compared to hM4Di, with peer reviewers noting decline to 50% after 2 years.
Strong agreement on expression decline after 2-3 years (C6, C35, C58). Both evaluations treat this as a novel and significant finding with important implications for the field.

Strong agreement on functional efficacy (C7, C41-C45, C57). Both evaluations emphasize the 2-year efficacy window supported by multiple assessment methods (behavioral, electrophysiology, FDG-PET), with peer reviewers highlighting the value of multiple approaches.

Strong agreement on monkey #234 case study (C47-C50). Both evaluations accept the correlation between PET signal loss, functional loss, and histology as valid evidence, treating it as a meaningful data point despite being a single case.

Strong agreement on protein tag effects (C8, C9, C52-C54). Both evaluations affirm the significant influence of protein tags on peak expression (P<0.008), with peer reviewers emphasizing the importance for viral construct design.

Strong agreement on sample size and methodology (C3, C28). Both evaluations note the impressive sample size (20 monkeys) as notable and valuable, with OpenEval describing standard PET imaging methodology and peer reviewers calling it 'an impressive accumulation of work.'

Strong agreement on PET methodology (C30, C31). Both evaluations endorse the imaging approach, with OpenEval noting standard methodology and peer reviewers emphasizing translational relevance and the selective radiotracer c11-DCZ.

Strong agreement on PET methodology advantages (C27, C84). Both evaluations support the non-invasive imaging approach, with OpenEval noting balanced discussion of advantages/limitations and peer reviewers highlighting translational impact.

Strong agreement on study limitations (C85-C87). Both evaluations accept the acknowledged limitations of retrospective design and variability, with peer reviewers viewing the transparency positively and noting the data was 'judiciously used.'

Strong agreement on agonist administration analysis (C38). Both evaluations accept the statistical finding that agonist administration did not significantly affect expression fluctuations, with no methodological concerns raised.

Strong agreement on histological findings (C65, C66). Both evaluations accept that neuronal loss was ruled out as a mechanism for expression decline, treating the histological evidence as valid without challenge.

Strong agreement on practical recommendations (C59, C77, C101, C102). Both evaluations endorse the 2-year planning window recommendation, with peer reviewers emphasizing this will inform 'experimental designs of highly impactful chemogenetic studies.'

Agreement on sample size for functional efficacy (C40). Both evaluations note the 17 monkeys used for functional assessment as part of the comprehensive dataset, with peer reviewers emphasizing the impressive scale.
Agreement on PET-functional correlation (C70). Both evaluations accept the correlation between PET imaging and functional outcomes demonstrated in the study, supporting translational applications.

OpenEval evaluates titer range rationale (C78-C80, C95-C96), explaining why titer was not significant in analysis due to restricted range. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific claims about titer selection and statistical interpretation.

OpenEval evaluates background and knowledge gap (C1-C2, C10-C17, C92-C94), affirming the literature review and rationale for the study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates protein tag contextualization (C81-C83), discussing consistency with prior literature and IRES-GFP constructs. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these contextual claims about tags.

OpenEval evaluates translational discussion (C68-C69, C107-C109, C113) regarding therapeutic applications and human gene therapy. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these translational claims, though peer reviewers generally endorsed translational relevance.
